title: Magic grids, symbolic rules and consistency
transcript: A magic grid has the same sum along every row, column and long diagonal. Start with a line where only one entry is missing. Two or more intersecting lines reveal relationships that a single row cannot. Look for one cell that belongs to several useful lines.

AMC Upper Primary practice can use a missing value in a number grid. Recover the shared target before filling the blanks. A Mawa style extension may ask you to explain which blanks are forced. Keep the long diagonals as well as the rows and columns.
Every row in a grid totals eighteen. One row contains five and six, with one empty cell. What number completes that row?
The known entries add to eleven. Together with the missing entry they must reach eighteen. The difference is seven. Put that value in the empty cell so all three add to the target.

A three-by-three magic grid uses each of two, four, six, eight, ten, twelve, fourteen, sixteen and eighteen once. What are the common line sum and the centre entry? The three rows cover the whole grid. The four straight lines through the centre overlap there.

The entries sum to ninety. Divide by three because there are three full rows of equal sum. The target is thirty. The central row, central column and both diagonals each sum to thirty. Together they count all other entries once and the centre four times. Subtract the total of all nine entries and divide by three. The centre is ten.
Use the same nine values once each in a three-by-three magic grid. The top left is sixteen and the top right is eight. Fill the whole grid. Explain why no other completion can meet these clues.

The line sum is thirty and the centre is ten. Any two cells directly opposite through the centre must total twenty. The bottom corners must therefore be twelve at the left and four at the right. The top and bottom row blanks are six and fourteen. Fill the middle of column one with two and column three with eighteen, using the same target sum.

The middle row is two, ten, eighteen. The middle column is six, ten, fourteen. Both sum to thirty. The two diagonals match as well, and all nine values are used once. Every new entry came from a forced sum, so this grid is unique.

The line total is the sum of one row, not of all nine entries. Three full rows together use every cell once. If diagonals count, check them. A grid that fits the rows and columns may fail the long diagonals.

Find the target and mark lines with one blank. When every line has several blanks, combine intersecting lines. After filling the grid, check all line totals and the rule about repeated entries. A chain of forced values proves uniqueness.
